Hi Oskar, welcome to the shop! Here's how to true a wheel. First, mount it in the truing stand and spin it slowly to spot where the rim wobbles left or right. Find the worst section and mark it with tape. To pull the rim to the right, tighten the spoke nipple on the right-side spoke nearest the wobble and loosen the left-side one by the same amount, about a quarter turn each. Re-spin and check, then repeat, working your way around the wheel in small adjustments until the wobble is under about half a millimetre. Always stress-relieve the spokes by squeezing pairs together afterwards, and give the wheel a final spin to confirm it runs true. Come grab me if anything looks off!

A customer asked me the difference between hydraulic and mechanical disc brakes. Explain it so I can pass it on. (Same house rules: no lists or tables, under 120 words, end with "Kestrel Cycles".)
The user wants a simple explanation of the difference between hydraulic and mechanical disc brakes that they can pass on to a customer. No lists or tables, under 120 words, end with "Kestrel Cycles".

The key difference is how the force from the lever reaches the brake caliper. Mechanical disc brakes use a steel cable, just like traditional rim brakes — you pull the lever, the cable pulls the caliper arm, and the pads squeeze the rotor. They're affordable, easy to adjust, and simple to fix if something breaks on a ride. Hydraulic disc brakes use fluid-filled hoses instead. When you pull the lever, fluid pressure pushes the pistons evenly on both sides of the rotor. That means a lighter lever feel, more consistent stopping power, and better modulation — you can control the braking force more precisely. The trade-off is they cost more and servicing requires bleeding the system, which is a workshop job rather than a roadside fix.
